name: File System Access (read and write handles)
plain: Lets a site open files and folders and save changes back in place.
meaning: Gives a site read and write access to specific files or directories the person picks. Since Chrome 122 a grant can persist across visits, so the site keeps access to your folder until revoked.

web.api: showOpenFilePicker(), showSaveFilePicker(), showDirectoryPicker(); handle.requestPermission({mode:'readwrite'}); IndexedDB stored handles

access.prompt_ui: Picker chooses what to share; a write prompt appears; Chrome 122 adds three-way prompt: Allow this time, Allow on every visit, Don't allow. Installed apps skip the prompt.
access.persistence: One-time until tabs close, or persistent across visits in Chrome 122+ after Allow on every visit
access.revocation: Address bar icon Remove access, Site settings per-handle trashcan; auto-revoked after a background period
steps: Store handle in IndexedDB to reuse

limits.headline: Can open files and folders you pick and save changes back in place
limits.user_action: You click Open or Save, pick, then click Allow.
can: Open the files or folders you pick
Save changes back after you allow it
Keep access on later visits if you choose Allow on every visit (Chrome 122 and newer)
Skip the prompt when installed as an app
cannot: See files or folders you did not pick
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge on computers only. Firefox, Safari and phones do not have it.

story.what_it_is: Lets a site open files and folders and save changes back to them, once you allow it.

marketing.name: File System Access API
marketing.pitch: Google pitches it as letting web apps read and save files on your device, like native apps.

story.for_you: You pick a file or folder in a system window. The site may ask again later to keep editing it. If you say no, it cannot touch the file.
story.for_makers: It lets web apps replace installed software, so a person can use a browser tool instead of a download. Browsers remind the person and block sensitive folders.

use_cases.example: A web code editor opens a project folder and saves changes straight to it.
A web photo editor edits a picture and saves it where it came from.
A browser game creator opens a level file and saves it back as you build.
A web note app keeps notes as normal files you can open elsewhere.
A company web tool opens a spreadsheet from a shared drive and saves changes in place.
A web build tool writes the finished site to a folder you pick.
A phishing page asks for folder access to look like a document tool. Browsers refuse many system folders.

technical_bounds: System folders blocked (e.g. home, Downloads root)
Chromium only for pickers; OPFS elsewhere

abuse: Ransomware-style bulk edits if a folder is granted

history.change: Persistent permissions via handles in IndexedDB
